# Introduction \label{Introduction}

A recent seminar argued that oil price volatility and global policy uncertainty are spilling over into local equity markets, and that local portfolios should lean more towards lower-volatility stocks. This note tests that argument in three steps. Part A establishes whether local volatility has increased and whether it mirrors the global experience. Part B evaluates how our SafeCore fund has navigated volatility and what its factor exposures are. Part C studies dispersion and correlation, to gauge the alpha opportunity in the market since 2020.

# Part A: Has local volatility increased? \label{PartA}

## Data

Local index returns (Capped SWIX, Top 40, Mid Caps and Small Caps, in rand) are available from January 2015, so the analysis runs from January 2015 to September 2026. For the global comparison I use total return indexes in US dollars: MSCI ACWI, MSCI Emerging Markets, the S&P 500, the Euro Stoxx 50 and the Nikkei 225. To link volatility to uncertainty I use implied volatility (VIX, V2X, VXEEM), economic policy uncertainty (EPU) indexes, US bond market volatility (MOVE), Brent oil volatility and currency volatility (SAVI for USDZAR and JP Morgan's global FX volatility index).

Two data issues were treated. The global and European EPU indexes are monthly values repeated on every day, so all comparisons with them are done at a monthly frequency. The SAVI index is quoted as a decimal rather than a percentage on 109 days (mostly March to June 2021); these values were rescaled.

## Realised volatility

Figure \ref{rollvol} plots the rolling three-month realised volatility of each index. The shaded bands mark five market events: two South African political shocks (Nenegate in December 2015, and the March 2017 cabinet reshuffle followed by the sovereign downgrade to junk) and three global shocks (the COVID-19 crash, the 2022 Ukraine war and oil price shock, and the April 2025 US tariff shock). The COVID-19 crash dominates every series, with local volatility peaking above 50%. Outside of 2020, local volatility has been punctuated by shorter spikes, most of which coincide with the global events.

```{r rollvol, fig.height = 5.5, fig.cap = "Rolling 3-month realised volatility, local vs global \\label{rollvol}"}
Plot_Roll_Vol(Roll_Vols)
```

Figure \ref{calvol} shows the same story by calendar year. The notable recent feature is 2026: Capped SWIX volatility (about 21% year-to-date) is well above that of developed markets (MSCI ACWI about 12%) and much closer to emerging markets (MSCI EM about 25%). Local volatility in 2025-26 is therefore tracking the emerging market experience rather than the developed market one.

```{r calvol, fig.cap = "Calendar-year realised volatility \\label{calvol}"}
Plot_Calendar_Vol(Cal_Vols)
```

Table \ref{tab:regime} compares average volatility before and after 2020, and the share of days each index spends in a high-volatility state (above its own long-run 80th percentile). Including the COVID period, every index shows higher volatility after 2020. Once the COVID crash is excluded, however, average Capped SWIX volatility barely rises (from 15.4% to 16.0%), while the share of high-volatility days still increases (from 17% to 22%). The increase in local volatility is therefore better described as **more frequent volatility episodes** than as a permanently higher level. It is also smaller than the increase seen in developed markets such as the S&P 500 and the Nikkei.

```{r regime, results = "asis"}
bind_rows(
    Vol_Regime_Table(Roll_Vols) %>% mutate(Sample = "Full sample"),
    Vol_Regime_Table(Roll_Vols, Exclude = as.Date(c("2020-02-15", "2020-07-31"))) %>% mutate(Sample = "Excl. COVID crash")
) %>%
    filter(Name %in% c("Capped SWIX", "Mid Caps", "Small Caps", "MSCI ACWI", "MSCI EM", "S&P 500")) %>%
    mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ .x * 100)) %>%
    select(Sample, Index = Name, `Vol pre-2020` = AvgVol_Pre, `Vol post-2020` = AvgVol_Post,
           Change = VolChange, `High-vol days pre (%)` = HighVolDays_Pre, `High-vol days post (%)` = HighVolDays_Post) %>%
    Print_Table(Caption = "Average rolling volatility (\\%) and share of high-volatility days, before and after 2020 \\label{tab:regime}", Digits = 1)
```

## Home-grown or imported volatility?

Table \ref{tab:events} measures how far rolling volatility rose around each event, from the level just before the event to its peak during the event and the following month. The two local political shocks were short-lived: Nenegate lifted local volatility by about 6 percentage points, roughly three times the global move, but the 2017 reshuffle and junk downgrade barely moved local volatility at all, suggesting the downgrade was largely priced in. The three global shocks, by contrast, lifted local volatility by about as much as global volatility (roughly 8 to 9 points in 2022 and 2025, and close to 40 points during COVID-19). The large volatility episodes in the local market have therefore been imported, while home-grown political shocks have been smaller and faded quickly.

```{r eventtab, results = "asis"}
Event_Vol_Table(Roll_Vols, Q1_Events, Names = c("Capped SWIX", "MSCI EM", "MSCI ACWI")) %>%
    mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ .x * 100)) %>%
    Print_Table(Caption = "Rise in rolling 3-month volatility around each event (percentage points) \\label{tab:events}", Digits = 1)
```

## Does local mirror global?

Figure \ref{rollcor} shows rolling one-year correlations between weekly Capped SWIX returns and the global indexes. Weekly returns are used because the JSE closes before US markets open, which biases daily correlations downward. The correlation with MSCI ACWI averages around 0.68 and rose to roughly 0.9 during the COVID crisis: in a global sell-off, local and global markets move together, exactly when diversification is needed most. More recently the correlation with emerging markets has fallen, suggesting that part of the 2026 volatility is local or EM-specific.

```{r rollcor, fig.cap = "Rolling 52-week correlation of Capped SWIX with global indexes (weekly returns) \\label{rollcor}"}
Plot_Roll_Cor(Roll_Cors)
```

## Conditional volatility

Ljung-Box tests on squared returns strongly reject the null of no ARCH effects for all three series (p-values close to zero), confirming volatility clustering. Comparing information criteria, the asymmetric GARCH models fit better than the standard GARCH, so I use a GJR-GARCH(1,1) with an AR(1) mean and skewed-t errors. Table \ref{tab:garch} reports the key parameters. Two results stand out. First, the symmetric shock parameter ($\alpha$) is close to zero while the leverage parameter ($\gamma$) is large: volatility rises after bad news but hardly reacts to good news. Second, persistence is high (about 0.97 locally), implying a half-life of a volatility shock of roughly a month. Local volatility shocks fade faster than global (MSCI ACWI) shocks but slower than shocks to the broad EM index.

```{r garchtab, results = "asis"}
Garch_Out$Params %>%
    rename(Index = Name, alpha = alpha1, beta = beta1, gamma = gamma1, `Half-life (days)` = HalfLife_days) %>%
    Print_Table(Caption = "GJR-GARCH(1,1) parameters (AR(1) mean, skewed-t errors) \\label{tab:garch}", Digits = 3)
```

```{r sigma, fig.cap = "GJR-GARCH conditional volatility, annualised \\label{sigma}"}
Plot_Garch_Sigma(Garch_Out$Sigma)
```

## What drives local volatility?

Figure \ref{drivers} overlays monthly local GARCH volatility (standardised) on each uncertainty measure, and Figure \ref{heat} reports their correlations. Local volatility moves closely with market-based measures of fear: global equity volatility (correlation of 0.87 with MSCI ACWI volatility), implied volatility (about 0.8 with VIX, V2X and VXEEM) and oil volatility (0.70). By contrast, the news-based policy uncertainty indexes show almost no correlation with local volatility (0.08 for global EPU). Policy uncertainty appears to matter for markets only once it shows up as a shock to global risk appetite or to oil prices.

```{r drivers, fig.height = 6.5, fig.cap = "Local volatility vs uncertainty measures (monthly, z-scores) \\label{drivers}"}
Plot_Drivers_Z(Monthly_Panel)
```

```{r heat, fig.height = 6.5, fig.cap = "Correlation of monthly volatility and uncertainty measures \\label{heat}"}
Plot_Cor_Heatmap(Monthly_Panel)
```

Table \ref{tab:reg} formalises this with a regression of standardised local volatility on the offshore measures. The VIX and oil volatility are the dominant drivers, and the offshore measures alone explain about 73% of the monthly variation in local volatility. Adding local currency volatility (SAVI) barely changes the fit and is not significant. Global EPU enters negatively once the VIX is controlled for, but as the EPU and VIX are correlated this coefficient should be read with caution.

```{r regtab, results = "asis"}
Driver_Regs$Coefs %>%
    mutate(term = gsub("[.]+", " ", term) %>% trimws()) %>%
    select(Model, Variable = term, Beta = estimate, `Std. error` = std.error, `t-stat` = statistic, `p-value` = p.value) %>%
    Print_Table(Caption = paste0("Standardised regression of Capped SWIX GARCH volatility on uncertainty measures (monthly). R-squared: ",
                                 paste(Driver_Regs$Fit$Model, round(Driver_Regs$Fit$R2, 2), sep = " = ", collapse = "; "),
                                 " \\label{tab:reg}"), Digits = 2)
```

## Implications for Part A

Local volatility has not risen to a permanently higher level, but volatility episodes have become more frequent since 2020, and in 2025-26 local volatility has tracked emerging markets rather than developed markets. These episodes are largely imported: global risk-off shocks and oil price volatility explain most of the variation, and they arrive with high correlation to global markets and with strong asymmetry (volatility rises after losses).

Was the seminar right that oil price volatility and global policy uncertainty are spilling into local equities? Partly. Oil volatility clearly feeds into local volatility, but policy uncertainty only seems to matter once it turns into global market fear. For our funds, the practical takeaway is that the risk worth protecting against is a global sell-off rather than a rand shock, so any risk ballast (lower-volatility stocks, rand-hedge exposure) should be judged on how it holds up in those episodes. That is the lens used to evaluate SafeCore in Part B.

Three caveats apply. The regressions capture associations rather than causal effects. Because monthly volatility measures are persistent, the regression residuals are likely autocorrelated, so the standard errors are probably understated: the large t-statistics on the VIX and oil volatility remain convincing, but the borderline terms should be read with caution. Finally, local volatility is measured in rand and global volatility in US dollars, so part of any gap between them reflects currency movements rather than the equity markets themselves.
